Abstract. The growing demand for high-performance computing (HPC) is exacerbating its pollution 
of the environment, so we need to explore environmentally friendly and sustainable solutions. By 
collecting global energy consumption data for HPC systems, we have analyzed the energy mix and 
its impact on consumption to understand the environmental impact of HPC better and build a global 
carbon emissions model based on it. The model quantifies the ecological effects of HPC by 
integrating the carbon footprint of various energy mixes. At the same time, we predicted energy 
consumption in 2030 using a Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) network. We also simulate the impact 
of increasing renewable energy on reducing carbon emissions. Incorporating renewable energy 
policies into our model allows us to simulate their effect on carbon emissions and energy 
consumption and assess the potential environmental benefits. However, the practical application of 
100 percent renewable energy is still challenging. In addition, we comprehensively evaluated the 
impact of HPC on other environmental factors. Based on this, we recommend a combination of 
technological and policy measures. 
Keywords: High-performance computing (HPC); Environmental impact; Energy consumption; 
Carbon emissions; Policy recommendations. 
1. Introduction 
1.1 Background 
As Global speed in processing data has increased, there has been an increasing demand for High-
Performance Computing (HPC) for all intelligence fields within the last few years. HPC with a large 
number of computer clusters utilizes large data centers, which use large amounts of fossil fuels and 
electricity and therefore lead to huge energy consumption and, consequently, greenhouse gas 
emissions, directly harming the environment and climate change. Moreover, the energy demands 
from HPC can burden the local power grids as much as any other industry, impacting other industrial 
productions and residential life. The second problem is that these computer clusters have different 
environmental issues such as large use of cooling water, e-waste creation, and land occupation. The 
excessive use of HPC has production, livelihood and environmental consequences. The main purpose 
of this paper is to conduct a detailed analysis and modeling of various environmental impacts of the 
HPC, as well as to propose appropriate solutions in this regard for sustainable and healthy 
development of the environment and science and technology.

According to the International Energy Agency (IEA, 2024)[6], the United States (US), the European 
Union (EU), and China are the regions that account for nearly 60% of the energy used by data centers 
globally, which will be the focus of the data analysis in this section. 
4.1 Data Collection 
We use data provided by the IEA for the US, EU, and China, as well as information from the 
AKCP (2024) report[10], as annual energy consumption data for the US, EU, and China regions for 
our modeling analysis. These data are typically expressed in terawatt hours (TWh). Combining the 
energy mix of each area, including the proportion of electricity generation from various sources such 
as coal, natural gas, renewable energy, and nuclear energy, we used Hermite interpolation-a 
polynomial regression-a mathematical tool used to fit polynomial curves to the data points to build a 
trend model or to predict the results-to estimate the total energy consumption of the data center.

7. Recommendations and Advocacy 
We propose combining technical and policy solutions to reduce HPC's environmental impact. 
Adopting energy-efficient hardware, AI-based power optimization, renewable energy sources, and 
advanced cooling technologies like liquid cooling can significantly cut energy consumption and water 
use. From a policy perspective, stricter energy efficiency standards, renewable energy incentives, 
funding for green computing research, and mandatory reporting of energy use and carbon emissions 
can enhance accountability and drive improvement.

9. Conclusion 
In this study, we used polynomial regression to analyze current energy consumption trends. 
Different energy mixes are considered through carbon intensity. Further, we used a Long Short-Term 
Memory (LSTM) prediction model to forecast data center energy demand. Carbon emissions are 
expected to nearly double due to the growing demand for AI and the slow transition to renewable 
energy. Achieving zero carbon emissions will increase costs accordingly, highlighting the urgent need 
for more significant efforts. Finally, our model assesses raw trends, AI demand, and water use 
efficiency (WUE) improvements. Data centers consume millions of tonnes of clean water each year. 
Despite conservation measures by tech giants looking to achieve water-positive use by 2030, this 
figure is unlikely to fall over the next decade. In short, the environmental impact of HPC is significant 
and long-lasting. Our work may contain potential discrepancies or inaccuracies; we strongly urge that 
recommendations such as improving energy efficiency, accelerating the adoption of renewable 
energy, and advancing water-saving technologies be taken seriously to mitigate these challenges.

Abstract: The growing demand for high-performance computing (HPC) is exacerbating its pollution of the environment, so we need to explore environmentally friendly and sustainable solutions. By collecting global energy consumption data for HPC systems, we have analyzed the energy mix and its impact on consumption to understand the environmental impact of HPC better and build a global carbon emissions model based on it. The model quantifies the ecological effects of HPC by integrating the carbon footprint of various energy mixes. At the same time, we predicted energy consumption in 2030 using a Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) network. We also simulate the impact of increasing renewable energy on reducing carbon emissions. Incorporating renewable energy policies into our model allows us to simulate their effect on carbon emissions and energy consumption and assess the potential environmental benefits. However, the practical application of 100 percent renewable energy is still challenging. In addition, we comprehensively evaluated the impact of HPC on other environmental factors. Based on this, we recommend a combination of technological and policy measures.
